controls.correct_memory_policy: Keep the departure-airport choice unset until the current trip facts are known. Start with the airport the user names in the request; if he says SFO first, search SFO first. Include OAK or SJC only when the current prompt allows them or when they materially improve schedule, reliability, fare, or meeting/departure logistics. Do not override a current instruction to use a different Bay Area airport.

controls.opportunity_description: The user repeatedly names SFO as easiest and many booked trips start at SFO, but other episodes deliberately choose OAK when the schedule, nonstop, or same-day logistics are better. A naive memory could over-personalize one airport as a durable default.
controls.strongest_false_inference: Always default Jonah to SFO for Bay Area departures.
tempting_false_inferences: Treat OAK only as an emergency backup even when it has the cleaner nonstop or protects a deadline.
Infer the opposite from later trips and default to OAK whenever Southwest/nonstop appears.
Treat SJC as categorically excluded rather than only low-priority unless clearly better.
controls.why_no_stable_habit: The lifeline shows SFO is often convenient, but the user repeatedly accepts or chooses OAK when it solves a timing or nonstop problem. Airport choice is driven by the current departure location, call/meeting timing, carrier schedule, nonstop availability, and fare gap, not a fixed personal default.

controls.correct_memory_policy: For each trip, compare total door-to-door reliability: arrival time, connection risk, last-leg recovery options, rental-car timing, drive length, weather/dark-driving risk, and first-site commitment. Present the closest airport, larger alternate, and drive trade-off only when relevant to the current route; do not store a fixed large-airport or closest-airport default.

controls.strongest_false_inference: Always avoid small destination airports and use the larger nearby airport plus a drive.
tempting_false_inferences: Always choose the closest airport even if it requires fragile regional connections.
Always prefer nonstop-to-large-airport plus driving because it worked for some Santa Fe and Twin Falls plans.

controls.why_no_stable_habit: The complete lifeline supports a case-by-case airport strategy. Boise/ABQ/DTW sometimes beat the smaller airport or connection, but ORF, CRP, MDT, TUS, SNA, and Pasco are preferred when they better protect the site schedule or reduce ground risk.

If the schedule is unsettled, propose cancellable hotel structures or wait for approval. Do not auto-add or auto-remove an extra night from memory.

controls.strongest_false_inference: Always add an extra night or arrive a day early for work trips with site access or booth setup.
tempting_false_inferences: Always avoid extra nights unless the client explicitly approves them.
Always choose Sunday/Saturday arrival for conferences.
Treat Monday-morning or same-day arrival as unacceptable even when the first commitment allows it.
controls.why_no_stable_habit: The user adds buffer nights when a specific risk exists, such as a moved security time, crate inspection, early setup, or manager approval. He also rejects or removes earlier arrivals when the risk disappears. The durable pattern is risk analysis, not a fixed arrival-day preference.

controls.correct_memory_policy: Check and report cancellation terms for each booking. If the premium is large or the user asks for cheapest/stable terms, present the trade-off before selecting prepaid or refundable.

controls.correct_memory_policy: Keep the return open until current end-time facts are known. Select the return by calculating meeting/teardown/dinner end time, required bag pickup, drive or rideshare time, fuel/rental return, airport buffer, next-day obligations, and cost. If timing is uncertain, hold alternatives or use a changeable/refundable structure rather than storing a fixed late/early return default.

controls.opportunity_description: The user sometimes prefers avoiding late arrivals, sometimes chooses a later same-day return to protect closeout, and sometimes stays an extra night or returns next morning. A naive system could store a fixed return-time preference.

controls.why_no_stable_habit: Return choices repeatedly change with teardown responsibility, customer dinners, procurement/slip risk, and debrief end times. The user is not consistently early, late, or next-day; he wants enough buffer for the current itinerary without unnecessary airport sitting or extra nights.
